title: reactive kernel window, graded backpressure, and KV warmup smoothing
author: Priya Natarajan
description:
Motivation: Production streaming workloads showed intermittent first-byte spikes under mixed-latency clients and heterogeneous sequence lengths. Root cause analysis pointed to three interacting problems: (1) the emission window selection was too coarse for bursty arrivals leading to token batching tails, (2) a single-threshold backpressure policy caused under-utilization on GPUs with differing readiness, and (3) cold KV cache fills created transient latency cliffs during warmup. This PR introduces a reactive kernel window selector, a graded backpressure controller, and a KV warmup smoothing mechanism to reduce TTFB and tail latency without regressing throughput.

What this change does (high level):
- Adds a reactive windowing layer that chooses kernel batch windows based on observed arrival distribution and per-kernel readiness signals (runtime/kernel/window_selector.*). The selector favors smaller windows when jitter is detected and grows windows adaptively for consistent high-throughput streams.
- Implements graded backpressure: instead of a binary credit/no-credit policy, we expose three levels (green/yellow/red) and allow partial admission for yellow requests to co-schedule low-cost kernels while preserving SLOs for green lanes (runtime/scheduler/graded_backpressure.*).
- Introduces KV warmup smoothing: when a request misses KV cache, we stamp a lightweight warmup hint and spread rewarm work across subsequent microbatches to avoid large synchronous stalls (runtime/cache/kv_warmup_smoother.*).
- Adds metrics, tracing tags, and a small observability dashboard to track window sizes, backpressure state transitions, and warmup amortization.

Checklist: 
- [x] Design doc and perf spikes reproduced locally (ENG-9123).
- [x] Unit tests for window selector heuristics and backpressure scoring.
- [x] Integration perf bench and canary run (benchmarks/perf/stream_latency_bench.py).
- [x] Added tracing tags and dashboard definitions.
- [x] Kept API backward compatible; no user-visible API changes.

Detailed notes on approach: The window selector uses a short sliding histogram of inter-arrival times and a per-kernel readiness probe (kernel readiness = scheduling queue depth + warm cache score) to compute an "aggressiveness" factor in [0.0, 1.0]. Aggressiveness < 0.35 forces micro-windows (min_batch), >0.7 allows expanded windows up to the kernel's fast path threshold. This reduces token tails by avoiding one-size-fits-all microbatching under bursty producers. The graded backpressure controller scores requests with a cost estimator (sequence length, model weight, kv-miss probability) and maps them to green/yellow/red lanes. Yellow lane requests are admitted opportunistically when kernel slack is detected; if a yellow request would delay guaranteed green requests beyond the SLO, it's buffered. KV warmup smoothing attaches a short-lived warmup token to the first miss and distributes prefetching work into the next N microbatches to turn large synchronous cache fills into smaller amortized work.

Performance: Canary results vs main (internal canary cluster, n=10 runs, mixed seq lengths 16/64/256):
- Median TTFB: -14%
- p95 TTFB: -22%
- Overall throughput at steady state: +1.8% (no regression beyond noise)
- Cold-start single long-seq case: p95 reduced by 30% due to warmup smoothing
These numbers represent typical regressions/improvements observed in our perf harness. We also ran the standard regression battery to ensure no throughput regressions on long-running saturated workloads.

Testing & validation: Unit tests added for scoring logic and warmup amortizer. End-to-end bench added and integrated into nightly CI. Canary deployment ran for 48h with traffic mirroring from prod during low risk window; we tracked per-route SLOs and found no increase in error rates.

Backward compatibility and migration: Changes are internal to the serving runtime; no config schema changes required. We added feature flags (runtime.feature.windowing and runtime.feature.graded_backpressure) guarded behind rollout flags for gradual enablement.

Rollout plan: 1) disable by default on main; 2) enable in dedicated canary; 3) enable progressively on Hosted API for low-traffic regions; 4) promote globally if metrics stable for 72h.

Related work: complements previous microbatch and flush cadence improvements (see linked PRs) but focuses on adaptive selection and cost-aware admission rather than only pacing.

review_comments: Ethan Morales: Can you clarify how aggressiveness handles pathological oscillation? If arrival rate swings rapidly we risk oscillating window sizes and hurting throughput.

Priya Natarajan: We added a dampening factor and minimum hold time of 80ms for window changes. Commented the code and added a unit test simulating oscillation (see tests/unit/test_window_selector.cpp).
Sofia Kim: Graded lanes look good, but we should ensure metrics expose yellow->green preemptions for debugging. Would also like a tracing span when a yellow request is admitted opportunistically.
Priya Natarajan: Added metrics 'backpressure_lane' and 'opportunistic_admit' tracing span; updated dashboard to show preemptions.
Liam O'Connor: Small nit: use steady_clock in one place for timing. Also add a failure-mode test where KV warmup smoothing is disabled to ensure correctness.
Priya Natarajan: Fixed clock usage and added the failure-mode test. Thanks.
merge_outcome: squash and merge (merge commit fa3b8d2). Feature flags added and default off; rollout will be coordinated with SRE.
release_notes: runtime: add adaptive kernel windowing, graded backpressure admission, and KV warmup amortization to reduce streaming TTFB and p95 latency. Feature gated, off by default. See docs/notes/kv-warmup.md for operational guidance.
